newsitem.title: GREECE: New Greek PM wants country to work harder.
newsitem.headline: New Greek PM wants country to work harder.

text.p: Socialist Prime Minister Costas Simitis, sworn in on Wednesday, called on all Greeks to join his struggle to build a strong nation with a new role in Europe and the Balkans.
"The fight which is just beginning is not only our fight, it is a battle involving all Greeks, including those who did not vote for us," Simitis, 60, said in a televised statement.
"Everyone must put forward ideas and work to steer Greece into the 21st century, into a new role, a new image and a new voice," he added. Simitis won national elections on Sunday.

Earlier black-clad Orthodox priests chanted a blessing for the new four-year government. Simitis, followed by 42 ministers and deputy ministers, then swore an oath of office to President Costis Stephanopoulos.

A reserved technocrat who studied economics in Germany and Britain, Simitis guided the socialists safely into a new era when he succeeded party founder and legend Andreas Papandreou as prime minister in January.
Wednesday's ceremony marked the end of the Papandreou era, with a new-generation socialist leader and his own hand-picked cabinet setting out a firm pro-Western course.
Since taking the helm, Simitis has spurned Papandreou's wild anti-Western ways, which delighted many but left Greece isolated from EU partners, weakened internationally and heavily in debt.
He said challenges facing his government included European unification, a new role in the Balkans, and economic development and modernisation.
"The government aims to operate immediately at a brisk pace ... to take advantage of anything positive and fight everything negative," he said in his statement.
Political commentators had predicted the socialists would be torn apart after Papandreou, who forged the powerful party from various leftist factions after a military junta fell in 1974.
Revered by the left, Papandreou was elected Greece's first socialist prime minister in 1981. He was re-elected in 1985 and 1993 but resigned in poor health in January. He died in June.
Simitis, untested as a leader, quickly outmanoeuvred rivals and replaced Papandreou as prime minister. He showed his mettle again when he won a bruising leadership battle in June.
He cemented his grip on power with his third gamble, calling an early election. His solid win on Sunday gave him a free hand to rule and laid to rest Papandreou's ghost.

Socialist officials said he stamped out efforts to haggle over posts and flexed his muscles by removing defence minister Gerassimos Arsenis. He gave Papandreou's son George only the number two spot at the foreign ministry and later had to defend the snub.
Simitis shied away from the radical cabinet changes he once hinted at and mixed old-guard socialists with young reformers who helped put him in power.

Markets have taken the moderate cabinet as an indication of stability and continuity. The bourse closed up 0.82 percent on Wednesday at 970.77 and brokers said investors were eyeing the 1,000-point barrier with optimism.

Also reassuring markets, he kept his economic team intact, reappointing National Economy Minister Yannos Papandoniou, who oversaw inflation's fall to single digits for the first time in 20 years, and giving him the finance ministry as well.
Simitis renamed Foreign Minister Theodoros Pangalos, who has won respect for his skills but raised eyebrows for occasional blunt criticism of some EU partners.
Pangalos's first challenge will be relations with Turkey and a new U.S. effort to lessen tensions between the two NATO states stemming from their disputes over the Aegean and Cyprus.
